title: Realistic return expectations from stocks
subtitle: Realistic return expectations
openingQuestion: An acquaintance says: 'If you invest in stocks and earn less than 50%/year, it's not worth doing.' Is this claim reasonable?
openingOptions: Completely reasonable, since anyone who decides to invest in the stock market should expect to achieve this level of return
Reasonable if that capital is invested specifically in a group of bank stocks, which always guarantee a very high return every year
Not reasonable - long-term returns are usually around 8-12%/year
Reasonable since the common bank savings interest rate currently is also around 50%/year
explanation: The long-term average return (10-20 years) of stock markets worldwide, including the VN-Index, is usually in the single digits up to around 10-12%/year when averaged across both up and down years. Expecting a continuous 50%/year is unrealistic and often leads to excessively risky decisions.

diagram.label: Hearing stories of doubling an account in a year
The actual index average over many years
Including the deep-down years, not just the up years
Comes out to somewhere in the single digits to a bit over ten percent a year

realWorldExample.description: From its founding in 2000 through 2024, the VN-Index had years of strong gains over 40% (like 2006, 2017, 2021) but also deep drops over 30% (like 2008, 2022). Calculated as a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) over the long run, the actual figure comes out to around 8-10%/year - much lower than the 'everyone's making big money' feeling often heard during euphoric market phases.

quiz.question: Why do new investors often have return expectations much higher than reality?
options: Because stock returns are inherently fixed at a very high level
Because securities firms must guarantee a minimum return
Because they only hear the standout winning stories
Because finance textbooks present returns incorrectly
quiz.explanation: The 'only-see-the-winners' bias (survivorship bias) makes beginners only hear the loudly shared big-gain stories, while people who lost money usually stay quiet. This creates a distorted impression of what 'normal' returns can be expected.

quiz.question: How does compound annual growth rate (CAGR) differ from just looking at the return of one strong year?
options: CAGR only applies to bonds, not stocks
CAGR always gives a higher number than the best-performing year which is exactly why the two figures get confused
CAGR and one-year return are exactly the same concept
CAGR compounds the return across an entire period, including down years
quiz.explanation: CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) reflects the average compound growth rate across many years, already including the down years, so it's usually significantly lower than just looking at the single best-performing year - this is why expectations based on one 'nice' year are often inflated.

quiz.question: What role does a realistic return expectation play in personal financial planning?
options: Helps set reasonable savings goals
Only matters for professional fund managers
Guarantees the investor achieves exactly that return every year
Has no role since returns can't be predicted at all
quiz.explanation: Setting a realistic expectation (e.g. 8-12%/year average long-term for stocks) helps calculate more accurately how much you need to save/invest to reach a financial goal, while avoiding chasing unrealistic returns by taking on excessive risk, or giving up out of disappointment when actual returns don't match the 'rumors'.

quiz.question: A portfolio gains 50% in the first year then loses 50% in the second year. What is the two-year compound average return?
options: 0%/year, since the gain and loss offset each other completely
About −13.4%/year, since 100 x 1.5 x 0.5 leaves 75
+12.5%/year, taking the simple average of 50% and −50%
−25%/year, splitting the total loss evenly across the two years
quiz.explanation: Gains and losses multiply rather than add: 100 × 1.5 × 0.5 = 75, meaning a 25% loss after two years, equal to about −13.4% per year. This is why sharp volatility hurts long-term returns, and why you must look at CAGR rather than a simple average.

quiz.question: Why does a ranking of 'the highest-returning funds over the past 3 years' easily lead to a distorted expectation?
options: Because three years is too long a period to reflect a fund's current skill
Because a fund's return is always published before deducting all management fees
Because losing funds already closed, so they vanish from the ranking
Because a fund with a strong track record over the last three years is almost certain to keep leading
quiz.explanation: This is survivorship bias: the ranking only contains funds still existing, so the visible average return looks higher than the industry's true overall performance. Past performance is also very unstable - most leading funds in one period fall to the middle of the pack in the next.

keyTakeaways: The long-term average return of the stock market (including the VN-Index) is usually around 8-12%/year when compounded over many years, not 50-100%/year as commonly told in stories
The 'only-see-the-winners' bias (survivorship bias) makes beginners prone to inflated return expectations compared to reality
CAGR (compound average growth rate) reflects actual performance far more accurately than just looking at the best year
Realistic expectations help build a sensible savings/investment plan and avoid excessive risk from chasing unrealistic returns

practicePrompt.question: You're 30 years old and want VND 5 billion by retirement at age 60. An acquaintance advises you only need to save VND 1 million/month because 'stocks earning 50%/year is normal'. Using realistic long-term return figures (8-12%/year), is this advice trustworthy?
options: Not trustworthy - the realistic expectation is 8-12%/year, so the monthly savings amount needs to be recalculated
Completely trustworthy, since a 50%/year return is a reasonable and common figure for every investor long-term
Partly trustworthy, since even though the average return is lower, VND 1 million/month is always enough to reach the VND 5 billion goal
It doesn't matter since a retirement goal shouldn't be calculated in advance using any expected return figure at all
practicePrompt.explanation: Using a realistic 8-12%/year return instead of an unrealistic 50%/year figure gives a much higher required monthly savings amount - this is exactly why realistic expectations matter for financial planning.

summary.keyIdea: The long-term average return of the stock market (including the VN-Index) is usually around 8-12%/year when compounded over many years, not 50-100%/year as commonly told in stories
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: The 'only-see-the-winners' bias (survivorship bias) makes beginners prone to inflated return expectations compared to reality

application.title: Calculate your own CAGR
application.message: If you've been investing for a while, calculate your own portfolio's CAGR (compound average growth rate) and compare it against the market's long-term average of 8-12%/year.
application.secondary: Your own real figure matters far more than any story about a 50%/year gain you've heard.

sections.text: If you've ever heard someone brag about a 200% gain in just a few months from one stock, it's easy to form the impression that this is a 'normal' return that could repeat consistently. Reality is far more complex and modest.

Looking at long-term historical data (10-20 years or more) of major stock indices worldwide - the S&P 500 in the US, or the VN-Index in Vietnam - the compound average annual return (CAGR) usually falls around 8-12%/year. This figure already includes both strong up years (like 2017, 2021 with the VN-Index rising over 30-40%) and deep down years (like 2008, 2022 falling over 30%).

It's important to understand: returns don't arrive evenly every year along a straight line. There might be 3 consecutive years of near-flat or declining movement, then one explosive 40% year to make up for it. Expecting 'a steady 10%/year' is a simplification for planning purposes, not what actually happens year to year.

There are two main reasons. First, the 'only-see-the-winners' bias (survivorship bias): people who win big usually brag about it on social media, people who lose money usually stay quiet, creating a distorted impression of the true success rate. Second is confusing the return of ONE specific stock over ONE short period (which could rise 100-200% if picked right and lucky) with the average return of the ENTIRE MARKET over the LONG TERM - two completely different numbers in nature and accompanying risk.

items: Long-term average CAGR of the VN-Index: around 8-10%/year (excluding dividends)
The strongest up year can reach 30-40%+, the deepest down year can lose 30%+
The return of a single stock can deviate far (in both directions) from the market average
The 12-month bank savings interest rate is currently around 5-6%/year - a 'safe' reference point for comparing the risk-return trade-off of moving into stocks

left.label: Unrealistic expectations
left.text: Believing you can earn a steady 50-100%/year every year by 'picking the right ticker'. Leads to accepting excessive risk, using margin, and trading constantly to chase an unsustainable return.

right.label: Realistic expectations
right.text: Understanding that the long-term average return is around 8-12%/year, with strong up years and deep down years. From there, build a patient savings/investment plan, diversify, and accept short-term volatility to achieve sustainable long-term growth.

lines: Long-term stock returns aren't a path to getting rich quick, but a tool for sustainable asset growth over many years.
Setting realistic expectations (8-12%/year average) helps you be more patient and avoid unnecessary risk from chasing unrealistic numbers.
